questions.q: In MS Word, the keyboard shortcut to change the case of selected text (cycling through UPPERCASE, lowercase and Capitalize) is:
questions.solution: Shift+F3 cycles the case of the selection through Sentence case, lowercase, UPPERCASE, Capitalize Each Word and tOGGLE cASE.
questions.shortcut: Three states at your fingertips = F3 (the 3 helps you remember).

questions.q: Sending e-mails that imitate a legitimate bank to trick users into revealing passwords is:
questions.solution: Phishing uses counterfeit messages/sites to 'fish' for credentials. Pharming needs no lure - DNS is poisoned so even correct URLs land on fake sites. Spamming is bulk unsolicited mail; defacement vandalises pages.
questions.shortcut: Fake mail asking for credentials = phishing, the umbrella term.

questions.q: The decimal value of the binary number 111010 is:
The IP address 127.0.0.1 is used for:
options: Loopback testing of the local machine
questions.solution: 127.x.x.x (typically 127.0.0.1 = localhost) loops packets back to the sender's own TCP/IP stack for self-testing.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

___ you finish the project on time ___ you forfeit the bonus.
questions.solution: The sentence offers two alternatives — finish on time, or lose the bonus — so **Either ... or** fits. 'Neither ... nor' before two clauses would need inversion and would deny both. 'Both ... and' makes nonsense of the choice, and 'Whether ... nor' is not a pair.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

The coach said, "The trials may be postponed till next week."
options: The coach said that the trials might be postponed till the following week.
The coach said that the trials may be postponed till the following week.
The coach said that the trials might be postponed till next week.
The coach said that the trials must be postponed till the following week.
questions.solution: Two shifts in one line: may steps to **might** and next week becomes **the following week**. 'May be postponed' shifts the time but not the modal; 'till next week' shifts the modal but not the time; 'must be postponed' swaps the modal for its stronger cousin.
questions.shortcut: Modal AND time word must both move. Half-shift = wrong.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution: The narrative continues in simple past sequence ('His colleagues laughed at first; later that day, half of them ___ him'): **joined**. It is the only finite past form; *joins* breaks the frame, *join* lacks agreement with 'half of them' in past narrative, and *joining* cannot act as the verb.
questions.shortcut: Narrative sequence: second event after 'laughed' takes plain past — no perfect needed in simple storytelling.
questions.passage: When Arun was small, his grandfather took him to the village post office every Saturday. The old man (1) ______ a reply to letters from his brother in Pune, and he insisted that Arun add a line of his own at the bottom. 'A letter carries your handwriting, and handwriting carries your (2) ______,' he would say. Years later, Arun, now a software engineer, still (3) ______ that yellow ink pen in his office drawer, though he rarely posts anything. Last month, when his office announced a drive to send handwritten notes to retired employees, Arun (4) ______ to write fifty of them himself. His colleagues laughed at first; later that day, half of them (5) ______ him at the desk, writing their own notes.

questions.q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Free power encouraged Harish to pump more water than his crop needed
Diesel pumps are designed to use less water than solar pumps
questions.solution: Stated: fuel cost fell to zero, and he watered 'for longer than the crop needed'; later his borewell dropped. One step: the absence of cost led to over-pumping. 'Always damage' is extreme (the neighbours use solar pumps and sell power instead). Nothing says the neighbours dislike solar pumps. Pump design is not discussed — the diesel pump simply cost money to run.
questions.shortcut: Reject 'always' at once; then pick the option that links two stated lines.
questions.passage:
When Harish replaced his diesel pump with a solar one, his monthly fuel bill fell to zero. For the first time, he could water his fields in the afternoon without worrying about cost, and he did — often for longer than the crop needed. Two years later, the water in his borewell had dropped by several metres.

His neighbours noticed. Some of them have now joined a scheme under which farmers can sell spare solar electricity to the power company instead of using it to pump more water. Harish says the payment is small but steady. 'Earlier, extra sunshine meant extra pumping,' he says. 'Now it means extra money.'

questions.q: **Kalamkari**, the art of hand-painting or block-printing cotton textiles with natural dyes, is chiefly associated with —
questions.solution: Kalamkari ('pen-work') is practised at **Srikalahasti** (free-hand) and **Machilipatnam** (block-printed) in **Andhra Pradesh**.

questions.q: In the T20 World Cup 2026 final, India's opponent was —
questions.solution: India beat New Zealand by 96 runs at the Narendra Modi Stadium, Ahmedabad. Sri Lanka co-hosted the event but was not in the final.
questions.shortcut: Hosts ≠ finalists — Sri Lanka is the trap option.

questions.q: Who was the **23rd Tirthankara** of Jainism?
questions.solution: **Parshvanatha**, a prince of Varanasi (son of king Ashvasena), was the 23rd Tirthankara; his symbol is the **snake** and he preached four vows. Mahavira (24th) added Brahmacharya.

questions.q: India's new series of national accounts (GDP) released on 27 February 2026 has which base year?
questions.solution: MoSPI released the **GDP series with base year 2022-23** on 27 February 2026 (replacing 2011-12), with a far larger deflator set. IIP followed the same base from 1 June 2026; CPI uses calendar year 2024.
questions.shortcut: New GDP/IIP base = 2022-23; new CPI base = 2024.

questions.q: What is the LCM of 16, 24 and 36?
questions.shortcut: 72 uses $2^3$ (one 2 short); 288 is a common multiple but not the least.

questions.q: If $a+b+c=6$, $a^2+b^2+c^2=14$ and $a^3+b^3+c^3=36$, then the value of $abc$ is:
questions.shortcut: Guess small integers: $1,2,3$ have sum 6, squares 14, cubes 36 — so $abc=6$. Verify one condition beyond the given sum before trusting a guess.

questions.q: A ladder 20 m long leans against a wall at $45^\circ$ to the ground. The height it reaches on the wall is:
questions.shortcut: Ladder is the hypotenuse: $h=L\sin\theta$. At 45°: $h=\frac{L}{\sqrt2}$. Trap: 10 is the $\frac{L}{2}$ guess.

questions.q: A dishonest dealer takes 10% more goods than he pays for while buying, and gives 10% less than the true weight while selling. His gain per cent is:
Select the related number: **RAM : 32 :: SHAM : ?**
questions.solution: R + A + M = 18 + 1 + 13 = 32 — the plain **sum of letter positions**. SHAM = 19 + 8 + 1 + 13 = **41**.

questions.q: Select the related number: **A : 2 :: D : ?**
questions.solution: A is 1st and 2 = 2 × 1 — **twice the position**. D is 4th, so 2 × 4 = **8**.

questions.q: **R is the father of S. T is the sister of S.** How is **T related to R**?
questions.solution: T and S share the parent R, so R → T as well. T is one arrow down from R and female → his **daughter**. (Niece needs T to be a sibling's child.)
questions.shortcut: Siblings hang under the same arrow; one arrow down + female = daughter.

questions.q: Select the related letters: **EHKN : GJMP :: RUXA : ?**
questions.solution: E→G, H→J, K→M, N→P: every letter moves **+2**. Apply +2 to RUXA: R→T, U→W, X→Z, A→C → **TWZC** (A wraps past Z).
questions.shortcut: Subtract positions slot by slot; a flat tuple means one shift for all letters.
